title: KPI trees
summary: Break one big number into the smaller numbers that move it, so you know exactly where to act.

lessons.title: What a KPI tree is
teach: A KPI tree starts with one big number at the top, like weekly orders. Under it you put the smaller numbers that make it up.
Often the branches multiply: weekly orders = active buyers x orders per buyer. Each branch can be split again.
The tree tells you where to look when the big number moves, and which team owns which branch.

questions.prompt: Pick the 2 numbers that multiply to give Uber's weekly trips.
options: Number of cities in the ads
questions.explain: Trips = riders x trips per rider. The other options matter less directly or not at all.

questions.prompt: In a KPI tree, the branches under a number should explain how that number is made.
questions.explain: Each level breaks the one above into parts. If a child number can't move the parent, it doesn't belong there.

questions.prompt: Put these from the top of Swiggy's tree to the bottom.
steps: Share of app opens that end in an order
Share of orders that fail at payment
questions.explain: Each step is a smaller part of the one above it. Payment failures cut conversion, which cuts orders per user.

questions.prompt: Why build a KPI tree?
options: To see which smaller number to fix when the big one moves
questions.explain: If orders drop, the tree points you to the branch that moved, for example fewer new users or fewer repeat orders.

questions.prompt: One branch does not belong under 'Netflix hours watched'. Which?
lines: Number of shows started that get finished
questions.explain: Offices don't change how much people watch. The others all feed hours watched.

questions.prompt: Match each top number to a sensible first split.

pairs.right: Active buyers x orders per buyer
Active users x messages per user

questions.explain: Most first splits are 'how many people' times 'how much each one does'.

questions.prompt: A KPI tree should go many levels deep before it is useful.
questions.explain: Two or three levels is usually enough. Go deeper only where you need to find a problem.

lessons.title: Splitting the big number
teach: Two common ways to split: by formula (people x frequency x value) and by type (new users vs returning users).
A good split is 'MECE': the parts don't overlap and together they cover everything.
Example: active users = new users this month + users who came back + users who returned after leaving.

questions.prompt: Which split of 'monthly active users' has no overlap and misses nothing?
options: New, returning and come back users
Happy users and users in Delhi
Users who saw an ad and users who like cats
questions.explain: Every active user is exactly one of new, returning or come back. The other splits overlap or leave people out.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 parts that multiply to give an online store's revenue.
questions.explain: Revenue = visitors x conversion x order value. A classic e-commerce split.

questions.prompt: 'Users on iPhone' and 'users in Mumbai' is a clean split with no overlap.
questions.explain: A Mumbai user can have an iPhone, so they would be counted twice. Split by one thing at a time.

questions.prompt: Which split is broken?
lines: Orders = new customer orders + repeat customer orders
Revenue = subscription revenue + ad revenue + other revenue
questions.explain: Happy and Android overlap and don't cover everyone. The other splits are clean.

questions.prompt: Match each split style to an example.
questions.explain: All three are useful. Pick the one that helps answer your question.

questions.prompt: Zomato's orders drop. Splitting into new vs repeat users shows repeat orders fell. What next?
options: Spend more on ads for new users
Split repeat orders further, for example by city or restaurant type
questions.explain: Keep splitting the branch that moved until you find the cause.

questions.prompt: Put the steps to build a tree in order.
steps: Split it into 2 to 4 parts with no overlap
Check the parts add up or multiply to the top
Split the most important part again
questions.explain: Start at the top, split cleanly, check, then go deeper where it matters.

lessons.title: Inputs and outputs
teach: Output metrics are results, like revenue. You can't move them directly. Input metrics are things teams can change today, like delivery time.
The bottom of a good KPI tree is made of inputs. That's where teams actually work.
Amazon is famous for focusing teams on inputs like price, selection and delivery speed, trusting that outputs like sales will follow.

questions.prompt: Sort each metric as input or output.
questions.explain: Teams change delivery time and stock directly. Revenue is a result of many inputs.

questions.prompt: A team should be given an output like 'total revenue' as its only goal.
questions.explain: Revenue depends on many teams. Give each team an input it controls, like search success rate.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 inputs a quick delivery app team can change this week.
options: How often items are out of stock
questions.explain: Stock, speed and accuracy are inputs teams work on. Revenue and valuation are results.

questions.prompt: Which is an input metric for Spotify's search team?
options: Share of searches that end in a song being played
questions.explain: The search team can improve this directly, and it feeds listening time higher up the tree.

questions.prompt: Which is not an input a product team controls?
questions.explain: Interest rates come from the central bank. The others can be changed by the team.

questions.prompt: Put Amazon's flywheel inputs and output in a logical order.
questions.explain: Inputs improve experience, which brings customers, which attracts sellers, which adds selection again.

questions.prompt: Why do bottom branches matter most for daily work?
options: Teams can act on them directly
questions.explain: The top shows if you are winning. The bottom shows what to do on Monday.

lessons.title: Build a full tree
teach: Let's put it together. Start from the north star, split into 2 to 4 drivers, then split each driver into inputs teams own.
Add guardrails beside the tree: numbers you will not let get worse.
In interviews, say the tree out loud: 'Weekly orders is buyers times orders per buyer. Buyers splits into new and returning...'

questions.prompt: Airbnb's north star is nights booked. Pick the 3 direct drivers.
options: Share of searches that turn into a booking
Number of Airbnb ads on TV
questions.explain: Nights = searchers x booking rate x nights per booking. TV ads are further away, photo size even more.

questions.prompt: Now split 'share of searches that become a booking'. Pick the 3 inputs.
options: Number of homes available on the dates
questions.explain: Guests book when there is a good, fairly priced, trusted home free on their dates.

questions.prompt: Which guardrail would you add to Airbnb's tree?
options: Guest and host complaints per 1,000 stays
questions.explain: Pushing bookings shouldn't lead to bad stays. Complaints catch that.

questions.prompt: Put these interview steps for a KPI tree in order.
steps: Say the north star and why
Split one key driver into inputs
Say which branch you'd work on first and why
questions.explain: This order shows clear thinking from goal down to action.

questions.prompt: Which line in this Duolingo tree is wrong?
lines: Daily active learners = new + returning + come back learners
Returning learners depends on streak keeping
Come back learners depends on reminder quality
New learners depends on lesson length
questions.explain: New learners come mostly from word of mouth, app stores and marketing. Lesson length matters more for returning learners.

questions.prompt: It's fine to say in an interview which branch you'd focus on and why.
questions.explain: Interviewers want judgement, not just a tree. Pick the branch with the biggest gap or easiest win.

questions.prompt: Match each Zepto branch to the team that owns it.
questions.explain: A good tree makes ownership clear, so each team knows its number.
